extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and constructions for maps to projective/quasiprojective schemes (via line bundles and sections), related notions (very ample / ample / base-point-free), gluing schemes, and the Curve-to-Projective extension theorem. Focused on when maps exist, extend, or are embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection formula (Exercise 16.3.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural morphism (π_*F) ⊗ G → π_*(F ⊗ π^*G) for π : X → Y and quasicoherent sheaves F on X, G on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the natural morphism; (b) if G is locally free then the morphism is an isomorphism (hint: what if G is free?), (c) if π is affine then the morphism is an isomorphism. (This is an important exercise to be generalized later.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness (Remark 16.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is called flat if the pullback functor π^* from quasicoherent sheaves on Y to quasicoherent sheaves on X is exact (not merely right-exact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an incredibly important notion; it will be revisited and given an equivalent but better-looking definition later (Chapter 24); see Exercise 24.2.L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of pulling back ideal sheaves (Remark 16.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ : Y' → Y and X' := X ×_Y Y' with induced i' : X' → Y', then µ^*(I_{X/Y}) need not equal I_{X'/Y'}. Pullback µ^* applied to the closed subscheme exact sequence is a priori only right-exact, so I_{X'/Y'} is the image of µ^*(I_{X/Y}) in O_{Y'}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affinely one sees the ideal of the pullback is generated by pullbacks of generators. If µ is flat then µ^*(I_{X/Y}) → I_{X'/Y'} is an isomorphism (see Exercise 16.3.F for a counterexample when not flat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms to projective space correspond to invertible sheaf + sections (Important Theorem 16.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fixed scheme X, morphisms X → P^n are in bijection with the data (L, s0, ..., sn), where L is an invertible (line) sheaf and s0, ..., sn are sections of L with no common zeros, up to isomorphism of these data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally: morphisms to P^n correspond to n+1 sections of a line bundle, not all vanishing at any point, modulo global units. A coordinate-free version is given in Exercise 16.4.E; the theorem works over Z (or any base). One direction: given sections produce local trivializations and hence a map; conversely pull back O(1) and its coordinate sections xi to get the sections on X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of maps to projective schemes via pullback of O(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a morphism π : X → P^n, the n+1 hyperplane coordinate sections x0,...,xn of O_{P^n}(1) pull back to sections π^*x0,...,π^*xn of π^*O(1) which have no common zeros on X, and conversely these pulled-back sections recover π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful viewpoint: always think of a map to projective space together with the corresponding invertible sheaf and sections. See Exercise 15.3.F and the proof of Theorem 16.4.1 for the precise correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embedding criterion for maps to P^n (Exercise 16.4.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π : X → P^n corresponding to an invertible sheaf L and sections s0,...,sn, π is a closed embedding if and only if (i) each open set X_{s_i} = {p ∈ X : s_i(p) ≠ 0} is affine, and (ii) for each i the map of rings A[y0,...,yn] → Γ(X_{s_i}, O) given by y_j ↦ s_j/s_i is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a practical method for checking that a map induced by a linear series is a closed embedding (used to check Veronese/Segre embeddings etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-point-free linear series induces morphism to projective space (Exercise 16.4.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite-dimensional base-point-free linear series V ⊂ Γ(X,L) for an invertible sheaf L on X induces a morphism φ_V : X → P(V^∨).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the coordinate-free version of producing a map from n+1 sections; over a field one can interpret sections as coordinates on the target projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondegenerate vs degenerate linear series (Exercise 16.4.F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → P^n corresponds to L = π^*O(1), the scheme-theoretic image lies in a hyperplane iff the associated linear series Γ(X,L) is degenerate. A base-point-free linear series V ⊂ Γ(X,L) is nondegenerate iff the map V → Γ(X,L) is an inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular the complete linear series is always nondegenerate. This characterizes when the image spans the whole projective space versus lies in a hyperplane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a curve via hyperplane intersection (Exercise 16.4.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical definition of the degree of a curve in projective space: intersect with a 'general' hyperplane and count intersection points with multiplicity. For π : P^1_k → P^n_k corresponding to O(d), there is a hyperplane H with π^*H nonzero and the number of zeros of π^*H (with multiplicity) is precisely d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows agreement with other notions of degree (e.g., Exercise 16.4.G). One must define appropriate multiplicity; see Exercise 8.2.E and 18.6.K for related instances of Bézout-type statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segre embedding and external tensor product (Example 16.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For quasicoherent sheaves F on X and G on Y over Z, define F ⊠ G := π_X^*F ⊗ π_Y^*G on X ×_Z Y. In particular, on P^m × P^n the invertible sheaf O(1,1) corresponds to O(1) ⊠ O(1) and the complete linear series gives the Segre embedding P^m × P^n → P^{(m+1)(n+1)-1}. If L and M are base-point-free on X then L ⊗ M is base-point-free and one can use Segre to combine maps from L and M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets product maps and shows base-point-free-ness/tensoring behaviour via Segre; used to show composite embeddings using Cancellation Theorem and Segre embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing schemes along isomorphic closed subschemes (16.4.11–16.4.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given closed embeddings Z1 ↪ X1 and Z2 ↪ X2 and an isomorphism φ : Z1 ≃ Z2, one can glue X1 and X2 along φ to form a locally ringed space X1 ⊔_{φ} X2; this construction produces a scheme, and is the fibered coproduct in schemes in this situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: topologically glue underlying spaces and define structure sheaf by compatible germs; affineness and stalk descriptions are given in the motivating affine example (Example 16.4.12). The construction commutes with base change and yields a scheme; see Exercises 16.4.L–N for details and local affineness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties preserved under gluing (Exercise 16.4.O and Remarks 16.4.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1 and X2 satisfy certain properties then the glued scheme X1 ⊔_{φ} X2 inherits them: (a) if X1 and X2 are universally closed then so is the glued scheme; (b) if X1 and X2 are separated then so is the glued scheme; (c) if X1 and X2 are finite type over a Noetherian ring A then the glued scheme is finite type over A (hence proper is preserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the affine motivating example and use generators/relations to check finite type; note there are subtle negative statements too (e.g., gluing X to itself along disjoint closed subschemes can fail to produce a scheme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Curve-to-Projective Extension Theorem (16.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose C is a pure-dimension-1 Noetherian scheme over an affine base S = Spec A, and p is a regular closed point of C. If Y is a projective S-scheme, then any morphism C \ {p} → Y (of S-schemes) extends to all of C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension, if it exists, is unique (reduced-to-separated argument); the theorem is often applied when S = Spec k and C a k-variety. The valuative criterion for properness gives a variant replacing 'projective' by 'proper' with additional thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of hypotheses for the Curve-to-Projective theorem (Exercise 16.5.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the hypotheses in Theorem 16.5.1 is necessary: (a) projectivity of Y (counterexample with t ↦ 1/t to A^1), (b) one-dimensionality of C (counterexample in dimension 2), (c) nonsingularity (counterexample C with a cusp y^2 = x^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exhibit maps from punctured source that cannot be extended, showing assumptions are not merely technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central method for extension: 'clear denominators' (16.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend a map given by rational functions on a punctured curve, choose a uniformizer t at the puncture and multiply the rational functions by suitable powers of t to clear poles (i.e., replace fi by t^{-N} fi) so that the new collection has no common zeros and defines an extension over the puncture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples: e.g., [t^4 + t^{-3}, t^{-2} + 4t] → divide by appropriate power of t to obtain regular sections; strategy applied after reducing to the case Y = P^n using Theorem 16.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very ample invertible sheaf characterization (Exercise 16.6.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invertible sheaf L on a proper A-scheme X is very ample over A iff there exist finitely many global sections s0,...,sn of L with no common zeros such that the morphism [s0,...,sn] : X → P^n_A is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an equivalent and practical definition of very ampleness over a base; existence of a very ample line bundle implies X is projective over A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very ample implies base-point-free (Exercise 16.6.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A very ample invertible sheaf L on a proper A-scheme is necessarily base-point-free (i.e., global sections generate the stalks everywhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the definition: closed embedding given by global sections implies no common zero for the chosen global sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties: tensor products and Segre (Exercises 16.6.C, 16.6.D, 16.6.H, 16.6.I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various closure properties: e.g., if L is very ample and M is base-point-free on a proper A-scheme X, then combining the embeddings given by L and M via Segre yields a closed embedding, so tensor/Segre constructions produce very ample or ample sheaves. Similarly, products of very ample sheaves on X×_A Y give very ample sheaves on the product via projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embeddings given by L and M, apply Cancellation Theorem and the Segre embedding to produce the desired global embedding; see the given exercises for precise statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and equivalent conditions for ampleness (Definition 16.6.1 and Theorem 16.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : X → Spec A proper and L an invertible sheaf on X, L is ample over A (π-ample) iff one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (a) for some N>0, L^{⊗N} is very ample over A; (a') for all n≫0, L^{⊗n} is very ample over A; (b) for every finite type quasicoherent sheaf F there is n0 such that for n≥n0, F ⊗ L^{⊗n} is globally generated; (c) the open sets X_f (for f global sections of L^{⊗n} over all n>0) form a basis of the topology of X; (c') those X_f which are affine form a basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties (a)/(a') link to projective geometry, (b) to global generation, (c)/(c') to topology. These equivalences are central: use (a)⇒(b) for Serre's Theorem A; see further cohomological criteria (Serre) and analytic analogs (Kodaira).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness consequences and standard lemmas (Exercises 16.6.E–G and remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences and useful facts: (i) If L is ample and M any invertible sheaf on a proper A-scheme X, then L^{⊗n} ⊗ M is very ample for n ≫ 0. (ii) Every line bundle on a projective A-scheme is the difference (tensor quotient) of two very ample line bundles: L ≃ M ⊗ N^∨ with M,N very ample. (iii) If π : X → Y is finite and L is ample on Y then π^*L is ample on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: use Theorem 16.6.2 parts (a) and (b) and the finite-pullback argument via global generation and surjections; these are used repeatedly in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampleness stability under tensoring (Exercise 16.6.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is ample and M is ample or base-point-free on a proper A-scheme X, then L ⊗ M is ample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine ampleness/global generation properties and the criteria of Theorem 16.6.2 to deduce ampleness of the tensor product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian vs general proofs for ampleness equivalences (beginning of 16.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The equivalence proofs of the ampleness criteria are given first under Noetherian hypotheses; the only essential use of Noetherian is generating certain ideal sheaves by finitely many global sections. For quasicompact quasiseparated schemes one can remove Noetherian hypotheses by writing quasicoherent sheaves as unions of finite type subsheaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof structure: (a')⇒(a) trivial, (c')⇒(c) trivial, (c)⇒(c') uses complements of vanishing loci on affine schemes, (a)⇒(c) embeds X and uses existence of sections vanishing along closed sets, (b)⇒(c) uses that ideal sheaf of complement is finite type (Noetherian note shows how to generalize).
